Implementors MUST devise ways of preventing this from occurring." The earlier finding is fixed: operatorOrdered (inner_selectors.go) keeps the both-operator-fixed exemption only when p.policy.Priority != h.policy.Priority, and both priorities come from childPairPolicy, which resolves an unset 0 to dataplane.PriorityChildSA, so unset and 2000 compare equal as installed. TestRFC3948ConfiguredOverlapEqualPriorityRefused (10.1.0.0/16 vs 10.1.2.0/24, both 2000 and both unset) asserts TS_UNACCEPTABLE, the policy-priority fix text, no state or policy on b, a's two policies and one record; its mutant record (operatorOrdered -> return true) is verified. Distinct-priority operator overlaps stay legal correctly: RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1 "Thus, a user or administrator MUST be able to order the entries to express a desired access control policy." The SPD then sends every packet into one tunnel, which is no Section 5.1 confusion. A priority change restarts the peer (reconcile.go peerConfigChanged via reflect.DeepEqual), so the pairs are re-claimed at the new priority. Distinct if_id: selectorsOverlap (dataplane/policy_owner.go) returns false on a.ifID != b.ifID, and the kernel matches a policy only on its own if_id, so those are separate policy spaces. f87c1883ac touched no removal path. All eight records of this row are current.
